Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," indicates Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

According to recent reports, the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

In a recent development, chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Sources indicate that quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

It has been revealed that in the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

According to recent reports, many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

It has been revealed that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Fresh Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

It has been revealed that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

Industry observers note that "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

Tech Report: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • According to recent reports, the approach has already revealed fresh candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

According to recent reports, the approach has already revealed fresh candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

It has been revealed that this capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Industry observers note that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Sources indicate that mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Recent findings suggest that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Newly introduced Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Light plays an crucial role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Industry observers note that beyond identifying upcoming candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Sources indicate that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

According to recent reports, "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how important it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

According to recent reports, most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

In a recent development, easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

Recent findings suggest that standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are important to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

Sources indicate that data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

Flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with newly introduced tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

Ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other people simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

trackio is designed to be a drop-in replacement for experiment tracking libraries like wandb. The API is compatible with wandb.init, wandb.log, and wandb.finish, so you can simply import trackio as wandb in your code.

Because this database is reset if your Space restarts, Trackio also converts the Sqlite database to a Parquet dataset and backs it up to a Hugging Face Dataset every 5 minutes. This means you can visualize your logged metrics in a Hugging Face dataset at any time easily:.

Tip: you can set the name of this dataset by passing in a dataset_id to trackio.init().

Trackio integrates natively with Hugging Face libraries like transformers and accelerate, so you can log metrics with minimal setup.

No extra setup needed—just plug it in and start tracking.

It has been revealed that openArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt states Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

According to recent reports, pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid aims from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example highlights how little code a basic request takes:.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

In a recent development, the say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

According to recent reports, is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free looks or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for newly introduced accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free proposal, which has no commercial licence.

It has been revealed that can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid aims, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

According to recent reports, how do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

The hidden human intelligence of design

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service. They are solely focused on the result and say, “I could do that with AI.” Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility. We are increasingly seeing this in the architectural industry. And it’s more than just a feeling or a hunch. Recently, the U.S. Department of Education moved to alter the definition of professional degrees to exclude architecture. This demonstrates a serious misunderstanding of what architecture entails. The creative professionals delivering complex projects in the built environment are experts: systems thinkers choreographing designs that shape environments, cultures, and communities. DESIGN AND EMOTION Design decisions are interconnected, but that complexity is often underestimated. Changes made after work is underway can require significant rework and additional layers of coordination, impacting budget and schedule. Even seemingly small change requests can ripple through other systems and affect project value. Behind every built environment is a constellation of decisions and balancing acts that are invisible to the end user. A successful design blends noiselessly into daily life. When everything is working, and spaces are intuitive, comfortable, and almost anticipatory in supporting your needs, you rarely think about the creativity, imagination, and coordination behind each design and engineering decision. Architecture’s value is its ability to make us feel something as we enter a space before we even understand why we are experiencing those emotions. The reverence of a cathedral, the excitement of a stadium, the safety and security of a home—those emotional and physical reactions do not happen by chance. Each response is a specific result of a team’s design decisions. IMPACT VERSUS HOURS There’s an idea that generative AI can replace nearly any profession. This is a tough pill to swallow for those who’ve spent years or decades honing their craft. But this way of thinking raises a deeper question: Is worth measured by the visible impact you create or the hours you log? I know architects aren’t the only ones who experience this. Leaders in finance, medicine, tech, and other fields hear from people who see the tip of the iceberg and don’t realize how much is below the surface. When they don’t understand the extent of expertise, they don’t value it. They think it can be done quickly and simply. The final output is neat and clean. But the reality is that the design process is often complex. It involves researching, discussing, debating, ideating, innovating, finding common ground, and making decisions. One skill an architect learns over time is listening beyond the client’s initial brief, identifying added value to the design program. Early in your career, you treat a brief as a rulebook. Over time, you learn how to advocate for a vision often shaped by a process of listening, challenging, and refining. It’s notable for us to embrace productive friction, in life and in this discipline. It’s the moments that must be experienced, including moments of friction when we are challenged and must overcome some adversity, that are more formative and leave a lasting impact. 6 DESIGN AREAS REQUIRING HUMAN SKILLS Consider these six challenging parts of any design process that require human expertise: 1. Consensus building: While AI can pull data from multiple sources, it cannot negotiate and compromise with diverse stakeholders. People disagree. An architect is a bridge between clients, project partners, and city officials. Architects have to balance vision with constraints, and to resolve disagreements and conflicts among all parties. 2. Constructability and feasibility: It’s impressive when AI can generate a beautiful rendering in seconds. But what if the rendering isn’t practical or realistic? Architects must make the design come alive in the real world. They need to know, through knowledge and experience, how a design will perform when built, and to exercise judgment based on wisdom. 3. Intelligence beyond pattern recognition: Despite the word “intelligence,” does AI think? Or does it recognize patterns, relying on existing data to predict future outcomes? As today’s problems grow increasingly complex, the synthesis of this complex data to anticipate outcomes is a powerful tool. Where AI recognizes patterns, architects bring discernment, interpreting data through a lens that is contextual and time-sensitive, creating solutions tailored to the histories and needs of specific sites and the communities that use them. 4. Risk management and resilience: Architects are tasked with thinking about future stressors on a building. Based on historic precedent, they consider what long-term resilience is required of buildings they are designing. AI can’t assume that human element of taking responsibility and accountability. IBM’s training manual in 1979 stated, “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer must never make a management decision.” AI doesn’t understand that lives will be seriously affected if its design isn’t resilient; it’s imperative to leverage the tool responsibly. 5. Challenge assumptions as a trusted advisor: We want to assume the best of those we work with, but trust isn’t easy to build. It’s built through real-world troubleshooting and problem-solving. Sometimes that means saying no. Anyone who ever had a chatbot agree with everything they mentioned understands that AI often tells you what you want to hear. 6. Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability. When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s important we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective. Steven McKay is CEO of DLR Group.

📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.
  • Arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains.
  • To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

Arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains. Most evaluations to date have focused on general-purpose tasks like summarization, sentiment analysis, or generic question answering. However, scientific reasoning and programming are essential for a broad range of real-world applications, from education to technical problem-solving.

To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation. 3LM is the first benchmark of its kind, designed specifically to test Arabic models in structured reasoning and formal logic which are domains traditionally underrepresented in Arabic NLP.

3LM is made up of three datasets, each targeting a specific evaluation axis: real-world multiple-choice STEM questions (MCQs), synthetic high-difficulty STEM questions, and translated code generation tasks.

The Native STEM benchmark consists of 865 MCQs extracted from authentic Arabic educational content, including textbooks, worksheets, and exam banks for grades 8 through 12. Questions span five core subjects: Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Geography.

Each question is annotated with metadata including domain and difficulty (on a 1–10 scale). The data was sourced using a pipeline that combined OCR (including LaTeX math parsing via Pix2Tex), LLM-assisted question-answer extraction, and manual review. This dataset provides a realistic testbed for evaluating factual and conceptual understanding in Arabic models using real educational materials.

To introduce greater challenge and diversity, we created a synthetic subset of 1,744 MCQs using the YourBench pipeline. This component draws from Arabic textbook text, which is chunked, summarized, and used as input to an LLM-driven question generation system. The result is a curated set of questions focused on mid-to-high difficulty reasoning, including conceptual, analytical, and application-based problems.

Synthetic STEM provides an key counterbalance to native MCQs by probing deeper reasoning skills and minimizing answer bias. All generated questions underwent filtering based on clarity, structure, and content validity, followed by quality assurance via manual review.

The third component of 3LM targets code generation which is a growing area of LLM evaluation. We translated and adapted the widely-used HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into Arabic, creating the first code datasets that test Arabic LLMs on natural language prompts for programming.

Sources indicate that we used GPT-4o for prompt translation and validated the results with a backtranslation pipeline, rejecting low-quality samples based on ROUGE-L F1 thresholds (< 0.8). Additional human filtering ensured prompt clarity and correctness. The code and test suites remain unchanged to preserve scoring fidelity. Evaluations use the EvalPlus framework for pass@1 and pass@1+ metrics.

Each dataset in 3LM went through a multi-stage development process to ensure data quality, fairness, and representativeness.

For Native STEM, we collected Arabic PDF sources and applied a dual OCR approach to recover both plain text and math formulas. Questions were extracted using LLM-based chunking and pattern recognition, followed by classification into MCQ format with randomized answer order. Final samples were reviewed by native Arabic speakers with STEM expertise to confirm answer validity and readability.

Industry observers note that for Synthetic STEM, the YourBench pipeline was adapted for Arabic input. Source documents after ingestion were first summarized, chunked and then fed to a code-controlled generator for MCQ creation. We filtered out image-dependent or ambiguous content, and only retained questions within target difficulty ranges. The result is a set of clean, high-quality synthetic Arabic MCQs for STEM.

Recent findings suggest that for the Code Benchmarks, our goal was to isolate language understanding while preserving code logic. Prompt translation was handled by GPT-4o with verification via reverse translation. Code and tests were untouched to allow evaluation parity with English versions. The result is a benchmark where Arabic prompts can be evaluated directly with the EvalPlus toolchain.

According to recent reports, we evaluated over 40 LLMs, including Arabic-first, multilingual, and general-purpose base and instruction-tuned models. Evaluation was performed using both multiple-choice accuracy and generative completion metrics.

In the MCQ setting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct achieved top performance across both native (71.8%) and synthetic (67.0%) STEM subsets. For completion tasks, Gemma-3-27B showed the strongest results with 43.2% accuracy on STEM answers.

In code generation, GPT-4o demonstrated best-in-class performance on both HumanEval-ar (83.5% pass@1+) and MBPP-ar (63.6% pass@1+). These results highlight strong correlation (~0.97) between Arabic and English pass@1 scores, suggesting language-specific prompt quality has a major influence on model outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that we also examined robustness under distractor perturbation, revealing that instruction-tuned models are significantly more stable than their base counterparts. Prompt engineering and zero-shot design were also shown to meaningfully affect Arabic STEM performance.

We built the benchmark to be easily reproducible using standard tools:.

All scripts, configs, and evaluation pipelines are available in our GitHub repository, and can be adapted to evaluate any model compatible with HuggingFace Transformers or OpenAI APIs.

All three datasets are open-source and hosted on HuggingFace Datasets:.

If you use 3LM in your research, please cite us:.

Industry News: Why ‘you don’t have to use AI’ is the new AI pitch

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • Recent findings suggest that watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both cases, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers. At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in its Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a upcoming Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.” This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that users didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to. “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he mentioned, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.” Instead of a new Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to the Max conference, though it had no input on this column.) AI-optional doesn’t mean AI-free None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy revealed Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI users will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027. Adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents. The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io. All this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies. This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer. Now everyone knows kung fu My business is actually a pretty good example of this. I use various software, including Photoshop and Premiere, to help produce content like The Media Copilot podcast. But I’m not a creator per se, and I’m probably using only about 10% of the features that would help my use case. For many, that skill gap is the difference between subscribing and not. But an agent that bridges the gap could mean Adobe customers are no longer just enthusiasts and experts. Suddenly, we’re all Neo in the Matrix: Just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung fu. In fact, one of the Max keynote demos was more or less my exact workflow: an outside AI agent turning a long-form podcast into a batch of short clips for social media. There’s also an urgency here, and again, my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun off-loading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Often, it’s open-source software that gets the job done at virtually no cost other than the tokens I expend. And Adobe users can even employ computer use—in which the AI uses your machine, just as you would—to operate the software. It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day. In other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very notable to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat. Media’s version of the same customer There’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest “State of the Bots” report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025. Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can quickly parse the bits that are important and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption. But what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any company’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text, and the same goes for images and video: Audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at Max. But it needs to be in the right context. A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally okay, but you need to be careful with generative content. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s “Generative AI and News Report 2025,” only 12% of people said they were comfortable with news generated entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news produced entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar. Most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach new audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward. Getting the agents to pay up But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a new and potentially huge customer base that doesn’t want to use tools but is happy for agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations. Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net.

Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to the Max conference, though it had no input on this column.).

It has been revealed that none of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy announced Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI owners will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027.

Sources indicate that adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents. The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io.

In a recent development, all this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies.

It has been revealed that this is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer.

My business is actually a pretty good example of this. I use various software, including Photoshop and Premiere, to help produce content like The Media Copilot podcast. But I’m not a creator per se, and I’m probably using only about 10% of the features that would help my use case. For many, that skill gap is the difference between subscribing and not. But an agent that bridges the gap could mean Adobe customers are no longer just enthusiasts and experts. Suddenly, we’re all Neo in the Matrix: Just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung fu. In fact, one of the Max keynote demos was more or less my exact workflow: an outside AI agent turning a long-form podcast into a batch of short clips for social media.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also an urgency here, and again, my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun off-loading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Often, it’s open-source software that gets the job done at virtually no cost other than the tokens I expend. And Adobe customers can even employ computer use—in which the AI uses your machine, just as you would—to operate the software. It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very vital to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat.

According to recent reports, there’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest “State of the Bots” report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025.

Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can quickly parse the bits that are notable and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption.

Industry observers note that but what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any manufacturer’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text, and the same goes for images and video: Audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at Max. But it needs to be in the right context.

In a recent development, A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally okay, but you need to be careful with generative content. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s “Generative AI and News Report 2025,” only 12% of people stated they were comfortable with news generated entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news produced entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar.

Most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach new audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward.

But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a newly introduced and potentially huge customer base that doesn’t want to use tools but is happy for agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations.

Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net.

Latest Update: RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Recent findings suggest that usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden. Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it. And RTO might be making things worse. A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface. The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and men by advocacy group Co-operatives UK, 22% of women said they’d been asked to do paperwork outside their role, 21% had been asked to clean or tidy the office, and 20% had been asked to make coffee for senior leaders. Overall, nearly half (49%) of women said they’d been asked more than once to do something outside their role, such as making tea or booking a meeting room. Women have been highlighting the problem on social media, sharing their experiences and how they push back against the assumption that they’ll take on these tasks. One content creator, Alex Schudy, said she had noticed colleagues using what she described as “weaponized incompetence” to try to get her to take notes in meetings, often by throwing her a compliment to disguise it. In her video on TikTok, she said she let the “silence linger” when one colleague suggested she do it because her handwriting was neat and she was “organized.” She politely declined, explaining that she needed to focus on presenting her part of the meeting. Someone else was designated the notetaker instead. Another creator, Anna Kennedy, described in a video how much office housework she had come to realise women were doing — from keeping track of action items and chasing colleagues to making sure feedback was acted upon. “Things that keep the machine moving fundamentally, but are not rewarded or seen in a performance review,” she said. “I’m never, I swear to God, never seeing men doing this kind of work.” As more employees settle back into office life, many hope there have been changes for the better, particularly around work-life balance and flexibility. But some of the oldest workplace habits seem stubbornly resistant to change, and it’s time women stopped being expected to pick up the slack. Ultimately, they shouldn’t have to spend their working days doing the jobs that keep everyone else organized, only to be left behind as everyone else speeds ahead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Contributors: David Austin, Raja Biswas, Gilberto Titericz Junior, NVIDIA.

In a recent development, NVIDIA’s AI-Q Blueprint—the leading portable, open deep research agent—recently climbed to the top of the Hugging Face “LLM with Search” leaderboard on DeepResearch Bench. This is a significant step forward for the open-source AI stack, proving that developer-accessible models can power advanced agentic workflows that rival or surpass closed alternatives.

What sets AI-Q apart? It fuses two high-performance open LLMs—Llama 3.3-70B Instruct and Llama-3.3-Nemotron-Super-49B-v1.5—to orchestrate long-context retrieval, agentic reasoning, and robust synthesis.

The AI-Q reference example also includes:.

The architecture supports parallel, low-latency search over local and web data, making it ideal for use cases that demand privacy, compliance, or on-premise deployment for reduced latency.

NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Super isn’t just a fine-tuned instruct model—it’s post-trained for explicit agentic reasoning and supports reasoning ON/OFF toggles via system prompts. You can use it in standard chat LLM mode or switch to deep, chain-of-thought reasoning for agent pipelines—enabling dynamic, context-sensitive workflows.

Sources indicate that one of the core strengths of AI-Q is transparency—not just in outputs, but in reasoning traces and intermediate steps. During development, the NVIDIA team leveraged both standard and new metrics, such as:.

The architecture lends itself perfectly to granular, stepwise evaluation and debugging—one of the biggest pain points in agentic pipeline development.

In a recent development, deepResearch Bench evaluates agent stacks using a set of 100+ long-context, real-world research tasks (across science, finance, art, history, software, and more). Unlike traditional QA, tasks require report-length synthesis and complex multi-hop reasoning:.

The open-source ecosystem is rapidly closing the gap—and, in some areas, leading—on real-world agent tasks that matter. AI-Q, built on Llama Nemotron, demonstrates that you don’t need to compromise on transparency or control to achieve state-of-the-art results.

Try the stack or adapt it to your own research agent projects from Hugging Face or build.nvidia.com.

#57876. The future of live entertainment

The future of live entertainment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.
  • Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.
  • Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Change is in the air. Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us. Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater. Technology can do so much, including simulating interaction and placing nearly limitless entertainment at our fingertips. But it cannot fully replicate formative live entertainment moments like the collective anticipation before a performance or the emotional release of thousands of people experiencing the same unforgettable moment together. Human beings are fundamentally social. We are drawn to one another and transformed by shared experience. Gathering is part of who we are. That fundamental human desire places us on the precipice of a cultural renaissance. Throughout history, moments of mass disruption have repeatedly created the conditions for extraordinary periods of advancement in art, science, architecture, technology, and design. These moments force societies to question familiar assumptions and search for fresh ways to understand one another. We are entering such a moment now. In this emerging age of artificiality, human creativity will command a new premium. So will presence. The experiences we cannot download, automate, or predict will become more valuable precisely because they are real. For designers (and any type of creative), this is an extraordinary opportunity. We have the ability—and responsibility—to shape the experiences that define the next era of culture. 4 IDEAS TO GUIDE THE NEXT ERA OF CULTURE History demonstrates that people are remarkably resilient. When confronted with uncertainty or moments of radical change, we search for reasons to believe in what comes next, then adapt accordingly. What follows are four ideas that can help ensure this latest cultural renaissance is a period of meaningful transformation that unites people globally for a shared purpose: connection. 1. The importance of optimism  That instinct remains powerful today. According to recent research from VML Intelligence, 69% of respondents regularly feel hopeful about the future. Beneath the anxiety surrounding technological and cultural change, optimism persists. That optimism matters because hope rarely remains an individual emotion. People seek opportunities to express it collectively. Live entertainment gives physical form to that desire. Watching Lionel Messi with his foot on the ball in the 90th minute of the FIFA World Cup, a stadium erupting in victory, a concert audience singing a chorus with Taylor Swift, or a theater falling completely silent at the same emotional moment reveals something profound. Emotion becomes amplified when it’s shared. The most successful venues build anticipation and entice participation. They create the conditions for strangers to feel connected. As optimism becomes a defining force in the next cultural era, the places that bring people together will become increasingly vital expressions of collective possibility. 2. The return of real The renewed interest in analog experiences is already visible across culture. Vinyl records, tapes, and physical media have returned to prominence. Film cameras and Polaroids are reappearing at concerts and celebrations. Tactile pursuits such as journaling and knitting are attracting new generations. These behaviors are sometimes dismissed as nostalgia. But they represent something more consequential: a desire for agency and authenticity. It is a tangible connection in a world of infinite, algorithmically delivered content. People want experiences they can touch and remember. They want the imperfect and the unpredictable. They desire the unrepeatable. Live entertainment is the ultimate expression of that desire. No two performances are the same. No crowd produces the same energy. No professional athlete reacts in the same way in that critical winning moment. The possibility that something unexpected might happen is the source of its power. Designers are beginning to respond through spaces that encourage deeper presence and participation. Listening rooms, intimate performance spaces, flexible venues, and carefully choreographed social environments are creating new ways to experience music and culture together. In the age of artificiality, the real becomes rare. Rarity creates the ultimate value. 3. From experience to transformation This cultural recalibration aligns with B. Joseph Pine’s concept of the transformation economy. This is the idea that people increasingly seek experiences that change them. Businesses and institutions will increasingly be judged by what they provide and by whether the experiences they create feel meaningful and transformative. This is especially true in sports and live entertainment, where identity, ritual, and emotion are inseparable from the event itself. The 2026 FIFA World Cup offered a powerful expression of this idea. Supporters traveled from across the globe not simply to watch soccer, but to participate in one of humanity’s great, shared traditions. The matches mattered, but so did the pilgrimage, the gathering, the rituals, and the sense of belonging to a global community. The same principle exists at every scale, spanning the intimacy of a listening room to the collective roar of a stadium and everything in between. Each can become a place where human connection is forged, moments that become treasured memories. 4. A collective opportunity awaits The next era of live entertainment will be defined by how thoughtfully technology is used to deepen, not displace, the human experience. Our greatest opportunity is to design places that encourage people to look up from their devices, toward the performance and toward one another. Places that transform attendance into participation, audiences into communities, and fleeting moments into enduring memories. These places give physical form to the things artificial intelligence cannot manufacture; chief among them, authentic, spontaneous, and shared emotion. The conditions for a cultural renaissance are already here. Its character, however, is not predetermined. It will be shaped by the choices of many, including cultural and entertainment leaders. Let’s collectively embrace an opportunity to design and lead a new era. It’s one that doesn’t come often and can spark lasting impacts that will positively influence generations to come. Brian Mirakian is senior principal at Populous.

In a recent development, since the days of MySpace’s Top 8, social media has made it easy to hurt your friends’ feelings. Instagram, however, keeps people’ social dynamics under wraps from one another, with accounts unable to see when someone unfollows them. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has previously said the platform hasn’t introduced a “who unfollowed me” feature so that users feel free to unfollow whomever they please without fear of judgment or tension. But a fresh tool from Instagram’s parent organization Meta is shaking things up. Its AI assistant Muse has an apparently petty personality under its cute and cuddly exterior—and it’s happy to help users spot who isn’t following them back and then unfollow them en masse. How Muse can purge your Instagram Social media users have discovered that Muse can sort through the people they follow on Instagram and point out any non-mutual connections. Though third-party apps have offered similar features in the past, they’re notorious for getting accounts flagged and taken down from Instagram. Muse, as an in-house app, doesn’t pose the same risk. One Instagram user who tried out the feature, Khalil Roberts, told Wired about his experience using Muse. Roberts gave Muse the prompt, “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on Instagram, and can you unfollow them for me.” It quickly returned an Excel spreadsheet with 151 accounts that fit his criteria, then asked if he wanted to follow through on unfollowing them. Roberts was among the chorus on social media singing Muse’s praises for letting them purge such accounts so easily. “I just cleared 80+ chopped hos who thought I was a fan,” one user posted. “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG,” another user boasted, crediting Muse in a follow-up post. Meta’s secret menu Though Muse’s potential for pettiness is a much-requested feature, it’s only being spread through word of mouth. Meta itself isn’t advertising the capability—or at least not anymore. Every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot upgrade itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Sources indicate that then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

The example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Industry observers note that generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Sources indicate that quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

According to recent reports, each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand proposal. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

It has been revealed that what is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

According to recent reports, is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for customers. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

How often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Industry observers note that do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

Sources indicate that how many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

It has been revealed that the sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

According to recent reports, GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a major one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

We aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

Sources indicate that according to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.
